title: The verb engine
goal: Install the main engine of Italian: the three regular verb groups and their six forms — and see why the subject pronoun can be dropped.
bekal: conjugate *-are*, *-ere*, and *-ire* verbs for all six persons
ask questions without changing the word order

dialogs.title: Dialogo — Che cosa fai la sera?
dialogs.intro: Budi and Marco are waiting for the bus. Small talk that, without meaning to, uses all three verb groups at once.

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.text: Budi, che cosa fai di solito la sera?
lines.id: Budi, what do you usually do in the evening?
lines.literal: Budi, what thing you-do of usual the evening?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Studio italiano e guardo un film. Tu?
lines.id: I study Italian and watch a movie. You?
lines.literal: I-study Italian and I-watch a film. you?

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.text: Io lavoro fino alle undici. Poi torno a casa e dormo.
lines.id: I work until eleven. Then I go home and sleep.
lines.literal: I I-work until at-the eleven. then I-return to home and I-sleep.

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.text: Mangio al ristorante, dove lavoro. È un vantaggio.
lines.id: I eat at the restaurant where I work. It's a perk.
lines.literal: I-eat at-the restaurant, where I-work. is an advantage.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: E il fine settimana? Riposate un po'?
lines.id: And the weekend? Do you get some rest?
lines.literal: and the end week? you(pl)-rest a bit?

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.text: Il sabato lavoriamo tutti. La domenica chiudiamo.
lines.id: On Saturdays we all work. On Sundays we're closed.
lines.literal: the Saturday we-work all. the Sunday we-close.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: E la domenica che cosa fai?
lines.id: And what do you do on Sundays?
lines.literal: and the Sunday what thing you-do?

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.text: Dormo fino a tardi, poi leggo e ascolto musica.
lines.id: I sleep in, then I read and listen to music.
lines.literal: I-sleep until to late, then I-read and I-listen music.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Anche i tuoi amici lavorano tanto?
lines.id: Do your friends work that much too?
lines.literal: also the your friends they-work so-much?

lines.speaker: Marco:
lines.text: Alcuni sì, altri no. Dipende dal lavoro.
lines.id: Some do, some don't. It depends on the job.
lines.literal: some yes, others no. depends from-the work.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I see. Here's the bus, finally!

notes: **The subject pronoun is almost always dropped.** *Studio italiano*, not *io studio italiano*. Each verb form is already unique to its person, so the pronoun is redundant. It's used only for emphasis or contrast — look at *Io lavoro fino alle undici* in line three, where Marco really is contrasting himself with Budi.
**This is a habit to practice, not just understand.** English speakers tend to stick *io* everywhere, because English can't drop "I". It's not wrong, but it sounds like a translation.
**Negating takes just one word: non**, placed right before the verb. *Non mangio*, *non lavoro*, *non capisco*. There's no helper verb like English *do*.

**Asking a question changes nothing in the order.** *Mangi a casa* and *Mangi a casa?* have exactly the same letters; the only difference is your voice rising at the end. Good news: one less thing to think about.

**Il sabato means "every Saturday".** An article in front of a day name turns it into a repeated habit. Without the article, *sabato* means just this Saturday: *sabato lavoro* (I'm working this Saturday) vs *il sabato lavoro* (I work on Saturdays).
**Un po'** is short for *un poco*, and the apostrophe is required. It means "a bit", and it's one of the most common words in everyday conversation.
**Capisco** comes from *capire*, an *-ire* verb that inserts *-isc-*. This group is unpacked in the second grammar box — don't skip it, because it's full of very common words.
**Dipende da** = "it depends on". Notice *dal* in *dipende dal lavoro*: that's *da* + *il* merged. These merged forms are covered fully in Unit 10.

grammars.title: The three regular verb groups
body: Every Italian verb ends in *-are*, *-ere*, or *-ire*. Remove that ending, then attach the endings below to what's left.
after: Notice how much is actually the same. The *io* form is always **-o**, the *tu* form always **-i**, the *noi* form always **-iamo**. Three of the six rows don't need separate memorizing at all.
Only the other three rows really differ, and even *-ere* and *-ire* are near twins — they differ only in the *voi* row.
⚠️ In the *loro* form the stress moves back: *PAR-lano*, *PREN-dono*, *DOR-mono* — not *par-LA-no*. It's one of the quickest ways to tell a trained speaker from an untrained one.

grammars.title: The -ire verbs that insert -isc-
body: Some *-ire* verbs slip *-isc-* into four of their forms. No rule tells you which ones; they have to be learned, but there aren't many and they're important words.
after: The pattern is tidy: the insert appears in four forms and disappears in *noi* and *voi*. Once you've seen the shape, just follow it.
The most common members of this group: *capire*, *preferire*, *finire* (finish), *pulire* (clean), *spedire* (send), *costruire* (build).
Common verbs that do **not** follow this pattern: *dormire*, *aprire* (open), *partire* (leave), *sentire* (hear, feel), *offrire* (offer), *seguire* (follow).

sections.title: Verbs enough for your first hundred sentences

blocks.text: These thirty verbs, times six forms, give you a hundred and eighty sentences you can use right away. That's far more than three hundred nouns could do without a single verb.

blocks.title: Spelling traps
items: Verbs ending in **-care** and **-gare** add an **h** before *i* and *e*, so the hard sound stays hard: *cerco → cerchi*, *pago → paghi*, *paghiamo*.
Verbs ending in **-ciare** and **-giare** instead drop one **i**, so there are never two i's in a row: *mangio → mangi* (not *mangii*), *cominci*, *mangiamo*.
Both rules are purely about spelling, not grammar. The sound stays exactly the same.
